Descriptores benignos y ADNEX en una estrategia de dos pasos para estimar el riesgo de malignidad de tumores ováricos: validación retrospectiva en la cohorte multicéntrica IOTA5 Objetivo Estudios previos han sugerido que los descriptores simples benignos (DB) basados en ecografías pueden excluir de forma fiable la malignidad en una gran proporción de mujeres que presentan una masa anexial. El objetivo de este estudio fue validar una versión modificada de los DB y validar una estrategia de dos pasos para estimar el riesgo de malignidad, en la que a los DB modificados les sigue el modelo de Evaluación de las Distintas Neoplasias en el modelo ADNEX si no se aplican los DB modificados.

Métodos El estudio fue un análisis retrospectivo con datos del análisis provisional al cabo de 2 años del estudio Fase 5 del Análisis Internacional de Tumores de Ovario (IOTA, por sus siglas en inglés), en el que se reclutaron pacientes consecutivas con al menos una masa anexial, independientemente del tratamiento posterior (farmacológico o quirúrgico). El resultado principal fue la clasificación de los tumores como benignos o malignos, en función de la histología o de la información clínica y ecográfica durante 1 año de seguimiento. Se utilizó una imputación múltiple cuando el resultado basado en el seguimiento fue incierto según criterios predefinidos.

Resultados Se reclutaron 8519 pacientes en 36 centros entre 2012 y 2015. Se excluyeron a las pacientes que ya estaban en seguimiento en el momento del reclutamiento y a todas las pacientes de 19 centros que no cumplían los criterios del estudio de datos quirúrgicos y de seguimiento de buena calidad, con lo que quedaron 4905 pacientes de 17 centros para el análisis estadístico. En total, 3441 (70%) tumores eran benignos, 978 (20%) malignos y 486 (10%) inciertos. Los DB modificados fueron aplicables a 1798/4905 (37%) tumores, de los cuales 1786 (99,3%) eran benignos. La estrategia de dos pasos basada en ADNEX sin CA125 tuvo un área bajo la curva de características operativas del receptor (ABC) de 0,94 (IC 95%, 0,92–0,96). El riesgo de malignidad se subestimó ligeramente, pero la calibración varió entre centros. Un análisis de sensibilidad en el que se amplió la definición de resultado incierto dio como resultado 1419 (29%) tumores con resultado incierto y un ABC de la estrategia de dos pasos sin CA125 de 0,93 (IC 95%, 0,91–0,95).

Conclusión Una gran proporción de masas anexiales puede clasificarse como benignas mediante los DB modificados. Para estimar el riesgo de malignidad para las masas restantes puede utilizarse el modelo ADNEX. Esta estrategia de dos pasos es útil para el uso clínico. 摘要 良性描述符和ADNEX两步策略评估卵巢肿瘤恶性风险:IOTA5多中心队列的回顾性验证 目的: 以往工作已表明，基于超声的良性简单描述符(BDs)可以可靠地排除大部分表现为附件肿块的女性的恶性肿瘤。本研究旨在验证BD的改良版本，并验证用于估计恶性肿瘤风险的两步策略，如果改良BD不适用，则在改良BD后对adneXa(ADNEX)模型中的不同肿瘤进行评估。 方法: 这是一项回顾性分析，使用国际卵巢肿瘤分析(IOTA)5期研究的2年中期分析数据。在该研究中，连续招募至少有一个附件肿块的患者，无论是否进行后续治疗(保守或手术)。主要结果是根据组织学或随访1年期间的临床和超声信息将肿瘤分类为良性或恶性。根据预定标准，当基于结果的随访不确定时，使用多重插补。

This article's abstract has been translated into Spanish and Chinese. Follow the links from the abstract to view the translations. CONTRIBUTION What are the novel findings of this work? This study is the first to validate the modified International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) benign simple descriptors (BDs) and a two‐step strategy to estimate the risk of malignancy in adnexal masses. Modified BDs are used as the first step, followed by the Assessment of Different NEoplasias in the adneXa (ADNEX) model if modified BDs do not apply. The strategy had excellent discriminative ability but underestimated slightly the risk of malignancy. What are the clinical implications of this work?

The two‐step strategy is suitable for clinical use. A large proportion of adnexal masses can be classified as benign by the modified BDs without computer support. For the remaining masses, malignancy risk can be calculated using ADNEX. An ADNEX calculator is available online and as an application for smartphones, and is embedded in many ultrasound machines. INTRODUCTION Ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer death among women in developed countries. Patients with ovarian cancer treated in tertiary oncology referral centers have a better prognosis compared with those managed in general gynecology departments 1 , 2 , 3 ,

4 . Correct diagnosis is important to facilitate the delivery of optimal treatment. To help clinicians decide on appropriate management, mathematical models to predict malignancy in adnexal masses have been developed on cohorts of patients that underwent surgery. A well‐known model is the risk‐of‐malignancy index (RMI) 5 . The International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) group created and validated four models to estimate the risk of malignancy in adnexal masses: logistic regression model 1, logistic regression model 2, simple rules risk model (SRRisks) and Assessment of Different NEoplasias in the adneXa (ADNEX) 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ,

10 . Systematic reviews and prospective cohort studies have shown that IOTA models discriminate better between benign and malignant tumors than do all other models including the RMI 6 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 . The ADNEX model uses simple predictor variables and calculates the risk of four types of malignancy 7 . Some adnexal lesions can be classified easily as benign or malignant using the IOTA simple descriptors. These are based on easily recognizable ultrasound features and do not require access to a computer

15 . If a benign simple descriptor (BD) applies to a tumor selected for surgery, the tumor is almost certainly benign (> 99%), while > 92% of tumors to which a malignant simple descriptor applies are malignant 6 , 15 . In clinical practice, it would be logical to first apply the BDs. If one of these applies, the mass could be classified as benign (risk of malignancy < 1%), while if none applies, a mathematical model could be used to estimate the risk of malignancy. To the best of our knowledge, such a two‐step strategy has not been suggested before, nor has it been validated either in masses removed by surgery or in those managed conservatively.

The primary aim of this study was to validate the diagnostic performance of the modified BDs and of a two‐step strategy, i.e. modified BDs followed by ADNEX if modified BDs do not apply, when used in both surgically and conservatively managed adnexal masses. METHODS Study design This was a retrospective analysis of the interim data from the IOTA Phase‐5 study (IOTA5), an international multicenter prospective cohort study that is ongoing 16 ,

17 . Consecutive patients with at least one adnexal tumor examined with transvaginal ultrasonography were included. Surgery or conservative management was suggested by the ultrasound examiner based on the ultrasound appearance of the tumor (pattern recognition), symptoms and evolution of the tumor over time. Recruitment into IOTA5 stopped in December 2016. However, patient follow‐up will continue until each conservatively managed patient has been followed up for at least 5 years. The interim analysis includes patients enrolled between 1 January 2012 and 1 March 2015, and follow‐up data until 30 June 2017. A total of 36 centers in 14 countries participated in the study; both oncology referral centers (tertiary centers with a specific gynecologic oncology unit) and other types of centers. Approval was obtained from the ethics committee of the University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven, Belgium as the co‐ordinating center (B32220095331/ S51375 ) and from the local ethics committee of each contributing center (ethical approval numbers are listed in Table S1 ). The IOTA5 study protocol can be found at ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT01698632 ). The current report is written in accordance with transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD) guidelines

18 . Inclusion and exclusion criteria Patients were eligible for inclusion if they were at least 18 years old and had at least one adnexal (ovarian/paraovarian or tubal/paratubal) tumor on ultrasonography. We used the IOTA definition of adnexal tumor (lesion), i.e. ‘the part of an ovary or an adnexal mass that is judged from assessment of ultrasound images to be inconsistent with normal physiologic function’ 19 .

Cysts judged to be physiologic (follicular cysts, corpus luteum cysts) with a largest diameter < 3 cm were not eligible for inclusion in IOTA5. Denial or withdrawal of informed consent were other exclusion criteria. Pregnancy was not an exclusion criterion. For the analysis of this study, patients with adnexal tumors already diagnosed and in follow‐up in the participating center before enrolment in the IOTA5 study were excluded.

Ultrasound examination and CA125 measurement At inclusion, ultrasound examiners performed a standardized transvaginal ultrasound examination and registered clinical information following a research protocol. By design, the ultrasound examiners were blinded to the outcome. They were not actively blinded to clinical information, nor to results of biomarkers or other imaging, such as computed tomography, that might have been performed before the ultrasound examination. All ultrasound examiners ( n = 77) had passed the IOTA certification test ( https://www.iotagroup.org/certified‐members ). Most scans were performed by Level‐II or ‐III examiners and very few were performed by Level‐I examiners (level defined by the European Federation of Societies of Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology (EFSUMB))

20 . IOTA terminology was used to describe the ultrasound findings 19 . Information on predefined ultrasound variables was collected for each patient (Table S2 ). Using subjective assessment (pattern recognition), ultrasound examiners classified each tumor as benign, borderline or malignant and specified the degree of certainty with which the diagnosis was made (certain, probable, uncertain). The ultrasound diagnoses were based on knowledge of the typical ultrasound appearance of benign, borderline and malignant lesions and that of different types of specific adnexal pathology

21 . If there were multiple masses, the one with the most complex ultrasound morphology was registered by the ultrasound examiner as the dominant tumor. The dominant tumor was used in our statistical analysis. At follow‐up visits, ultrasound examination was performed following the same protocol as at the inclusion scan, and clinical information, including information on symptoms, was obtained. At each examination, the ultrasound examiner proposed management (surgical removal or follow‐up) based on the ultrasound diagnosis and the patient's symptoms. However, the final decisions about management were made by the referring clinicians, taking into account clinical symptoms, ultrasound findings, findings from other imaging modalities such as computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, tumor markers and patient preference.

Conservative management comprised clinical and ultrasound follow‐up at intervals of 3 months, 6 months and 12 months, and then every 12 months thereafter. Measurement of serum CA125 was encouraged, but it was not an inclusion criterion for the study. Measurements of CA125 were performed according to local practice in each center.

Data collection and cleaning Patient data were registered on a secure electronic platform (IOTA5 Study Screen; astraia software, Munich, Germany). A unique identifier code was assigned automatically to each patient. All data communications were encrypted to guarantee data security. Data cleaning was performed by a team of ultrasound examiners and biostatisticians. It included queries to local investigators to amend inconsistencies and complete missing data. A standardized questionnaire (Appendix S1 ) for patients and/or managing clinicians was used at the local centers to retrieve missing information. Before analyzing our data, we defined the criteria for a study center to be included in our analysis. For a center to be included, we required it to have recruited at least 50 patients, to have recruited patients consecutively, irrespective of suggested management (surgery or conservative management with follow‐up) and to have good quality follow‐up data for at least 70% of the recruited patients. We defined good follow‐up data as a recorded study outcome (surgery at any point, spontaneous resolution of the mass or patient death) or a last follow‐up visit at least 10 months after inclusion. The 70% cut‐off was chosen arbitrarily, because it seemed reasonable to members of the IOTA Steering Committee (details in Appendix S2 ).

Modified BDs and the two‐step strategy We modified a priori the original BDs 15 by requiring the largest diameter of the tumor to be < 10 cm for all four descriptors instead of only for the third descriptor (Figure 1 ). We refer to these descriptors as modified BDs. The size criterion was added to decrease the likelihood of a malignant tumor being misclassified as benign. Based on data from the IOTA Phase‐1–3 studies ( n = 5914) 6 , 1618 (27%) tumors fulfilled the criteria of an original BD, of which 11 (0.7%) were malignant. Among the same 5914 tumors, 1427 (24%) fulfilled the criteria of a modified BD, of which six (0.4%) were malignant (unpublished data).

UOG-26080-FIG-0001-b The malignant simple descriptors 15 are not used in the two‐step strategy. As a first step in the two‐step strategy, the modified BDs are used. When the modified BDs do not apply, the second step is to use ADNEX. ADNEX calculates the probability of five outcome categories: benign, borderline, Stage‐I primary invasive ovarian malignancy, Stage‐II–IV primary invasive ovarian malignancy and metastasis in the ovary from another primary origin (e.g. breast cancer or colon cancer)

7 . ADNEX uses three clinical and six ultrasound predictors: type of center (oncology center vs other), patient age, CA125 level, maximum diameter of the lesion, proportion of solid tissue, number of papillary projections, presence of > 10 cyst locules, presence of acoustic shadows and presence of ascites. ADNEX can also be used without CA125. Details on the ADNEX model are provided in Appendix S3 . Model predictions are based on information obtained at the inclusion scan and hence are blinded to the outcome.

Reference standard The reference standard refers to the nature of the adnexal tumor (benign or malignant) at inclusion. Borderline tumors were classified as malignant. Each adnexal mass was classified as benign or malignant based on histology, if the tumor was surgically removed, otherwise on the results of follow‐up examinations (see below). The histology of the surgically removed tumor was determined at the local center. Central pathology review was not performed, because we found little difference between local and central pathology reports in a previous IOTA study

8 . Pathologists were blinded to ultrasound predictor variables and model predictions but might have received information on the subjective assessment by the ultrasound examiner when clinically relevant. Malignant tumors were classified according to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) guidelines

22 . If the tumor was not surgically removed, it was classified as benign or malignant based on clinical and ultrasound findings during 12 ± 2 months of follow‐up (i.e. minimum follow‐up time to assign an outcome was 10 months). Different scenarios were possible: some patients underwent surgery without follow‐up, others were managed conservatively with or without surgery later. For some patients, we had no information from after the inclusion visit. If data to classify the tumor as benign or malignant at inclusion were not available, the outcome was classified as uncertain. Study endpoints In line with the study objectives, the main study endpoints were: (1) the percentage of tumors to which the modified BDs apply; (2) the percentage of malignant tumors among lesions to which the modified BDs apply; and (3) the diagnostic performance in terms of discrimination and calibration of the two‐step strategy. The secondary study endpoint was the discriminative ability of ADNEX (with and without CA125) when applied only to tumors to which the modified BDs do not apply.

Statistical analysis A summary of the statistical analysis is provided below. Details on statistical analysis and discussion of sample size can be found in Appendices S4–S6 . The statistical analysis was performed with R version 3.5.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

We calculated the percentage of patients to which the modified BDs applied and the prevalence of malignancy in tumors to which the modified BDs applied. To assess performance of the two‐step strategy, we needed risk estimates for each of the five tumor outcomes when the modified BDs applied. Appendix S5 describes how these risk estimates were obtained. We evaluated discrimination between benign and malignant tumors using the area under the receiver‐operating‐characteristics curve (AUC). To evaluate calibration of the estimated risk of malignancy, we calculated the calibration intercept and slope using a logistic recalibration model

23 . Clinical utility was assessed using decision‐curve analysis by calculating net benefit at thresholds for estimated risks of malignancy between 5% and 50% to decide which patients to refer to specialized oncological care 24 . For the two‐step strategy, we assessed further the AUC for each pairing of the five tumor subtypes, the polytomous discrimination index (PDI) as a multiclass AUC, and calibration for the estimated risks of each of the five tumor subtypes 25 , 26 .

For the percentage of patients to which the modified BDs applied, AUC for benign vs malignant tumors, calibration of the risk of malignancy and decision‐curve analysis, we addressed heterogeneity between centers. This was done by calculating center‐specific performance and combining the results using meta‐analysis (Appendix S4 ) 23 , 24 , 27 . Heterogeneity in the AUC was quantified using 95% prediction intervals (PI)

28 , which describe the range of AUC values that can be expected in a new center. Because the number of malignant tumors was too low, meta‐analysis was not possible for the prevalence of malignancy in tumors to which the modified BDs applied, AUC for each pairing of tumor subtypes, PDI and calibration for each tumor subtype. For these analyses, data from all centers were pooled. For the percentage of patients to which the modified BDs applied, we performed both a meta‐analysis and a pooled analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed for menopausal status and type of center.

Methods to address potential sources of bias We implemented several procedures to reduce potential bias. First, we followed a prespecified statistical analysis plan to avoid selecting analyses based on results. Second, to handle differential verification, we used prespecified criteria to determine whether tumor outcome was benign, malignant or uncertain (Table 1 ). Third, the primary analysis included all patients after multiple imputation of missing CA125 levels and uncertain outcomes (Appendix S4 ). Excluding participants with uncertain outcome leads to partial verification bias and excluding participants with missing CA125 leads to selection bias 18 , 27 , 29 ,
30 . Multiple imputation is a recommended approach to avoid such exclusions

30 . Fourth, we performed a prespecified sensitivity analysis, in which we expanded the definition of uncertain outcomes to include all groups in which subjective assessment of ultrasound images was used to label outcomes as benign or malignant (B2, M2,3 and U1–4 in Table 1 ). This was done to address possible optimistic bias due to differential verification. Fifth, we used prespecified criteria for data quality in order to include only data from centers with consecutive inclusion and sufficiently complete and accurate data (Appendix S2 ). This may limit potential attrition bias by avoiding exclusions at patient‐level (instead, we excluded entire centers) and limits the number of uncertain outcomes. Finally, an additional prespecified analysis was performed in which masses with uncertain outcome as per Table 1 were excluded. This was done for completeness only, because exclusions based on missing data result in high risk of bias

RESULTS Patient flow is shown in Figure S1 . A total of 8519 patients recruited at 36 centers were included in the interim dataset of IOTA5 (Table S3 ). Twenty‐five patients were excluded due to withdrawal of consent. Another 2777 patients from 19 centers were excluded from the primary analysis: one center terminated participation, seven centers recruited < 50 participants, three centers were excluded due to non‐consecutive recruitment and eight centers due to suboptimal data quality. Suboptimal data quality was explained by lack of staff (three centers), problems with information technology (two centers) and/or difficulties with making patients return for planned follow‐up visits (four centers) (Appendix S2 ). Of the 5717 patients in the remaining 17 centers, 812 (14%) patients had a mass that was already being followed up in the recruitment center before inclusion. Therefore, 4905 patients were included in our primary analysis (Table S1 ). In 4151 (85%) of the 4905 women, the ultrasound examiner's suggestion for management was followed, in 445 (9%) it was not followed and in 309 (6%) the actual management was unknown.

Patient and tumor characteristics are shown in Table 2 . Median age of the 4905 patients was 48 (interquartile range (IQR), 36–62; range, 18–98) years, 2151 patients (44%) were postmenopausal, 2140 (44%) had a dominant mass that was a unilocular cyst and 1734 (35%) had a dominant mass containing solid components. Median maximum lesion diameter was 55 (IQR, 38–83; range, 7–751) mm and 2031 masses (41%) had no detectable blood flow on color or power Doppler (color score 1). Information on CA125 was missing in 2620/4905 (53%) patients. Missing CA125 values were less common for patients who underwent surgery (32%) or who had a tumor considered probably malignant (23%) or certainly malignant (14%) (Table S4 ). In all, 3441 (70%) tumors were benign, 978 (20%) were malignant (borderline or invasive) and for 486 (10%) tumors the outcome was uncertain (Table S1 ). Uncertain outcome was explained by loss to follow‐up ( n = 432) or by conflicting information during follow‐up ( n = 54) (Table 1 ). Loss to follow‐up was more common when conservative management was suggested (13%) than when surgery was suggested (5%), and more common when the diagnosis based on subjective assessment was benign (21%) compared with when it was uncertain or malignant (16%) (Table S5 ). A smaller proportion of tumors in this study manifested malignant ultrasound features compared with the development dataset of ADNEX. This is because the development set included only patients that underwent surgery

17 . The modified BDs were applicable in 37% (1798/4905) of tumors (pooled analysis). Center‐specific results and the results of meta‐analysis are shown in Table S6 . Of the 1798 tumors to which the modified BDs applied, 0.7% (95% CI, 0.4–1.1%) were malignant: 0.3% were borderline tumors, 0.1% were Stage‐I primary ovarian invasive malignancies, 0.1% were Stage‐II–IV primary ovarian invasive malignancy and 0.2% were secondary metastatic tumors (Table 3 ). Among the 3107 patients with a tumor to which the modified BDs did not apply, the AUC for ADNEX with CA125 was 0.92 (95% CI, 0.89–0.94; 95% PI, 0.80–0.97) and for ADNEX without CA125 it was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.87–0.93; 95% PI, 0.78–0.96).

Uncertain tumor outcomes were multiply imputed. Results averaged over imputed datasets, hence the decimals for the number of tumors of each type. There are no decimals for the overall n values because data needed for modified BDs did not have missing data.

The overall AUCs for the two‐step strategy were 0.95 (95% CI, 0.92–0.96; 95% PI, 0.85–0.98) when ADNEX with CA125 was used as the second step and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.92–0.96; 95% PI, 0.84–0.98) when ADNEX without CA125 was used (Figure 2 ). Sensitivity and specificity of the two‐step strategies when using different risk cut‐offs to indicate malignancy are shown in Table S7 . The overall calibration curves for the two‐step strategies are shown in Figure 3 . Risk estimates were slightly underestimated and heterogeneity between centers was observed (Figure S2 ). The summary decision curves of the two‐step strategies overlapped completely with the curves showing the results when using ADNEX in all tumors (Figure 4 ).

UOG-26080-FIG-0004-c The ability of the two‐step strategies to discriminate between different tumor types is shown in Table S8 . With two exceptions, the two‐step strategies manifested similar discriminative ability: using ADNEX with CA125 as the second step instead of ADNEX without CA125 discriminated better between Stage‐II–IV and Stage‐I ovarian malignancy (AUC, 0.81 vs 0.72) and between Stage‐II–IV ovarian malignancy and metastases (AUC, 0.76 vs 0.64). For discrimination between benign tumors and each malignant subtype, AUCs ranged from 0.91 to 0.98. Calibration of the predicted risks for the five subgroups of tumor was good for both two‐step strategies, albeit with some underestimation of the risk of secondary metastasis (Figure S3 ).

Subgroup analyses The modified BDs were applicable less often in postmenopausal women (24%, 509/2151) compared with premenopausal women (47%, 1289/2754), and the prevalence of malignancy among tumors to which a modified BD applied was higher in postmenopausal compared with premenopausal women (1.0% vs 0.5%) (Table S9 ). The modified BDs were applicable less often in patients examined in oncology centers (33%, 1020/3094) compared with those examined in non‐oncology centers (43%, 778/1811), and the prevalence of malignancy among tumors to which a modified BD applied was higher in oncology centers compared with in non‐oncology centers (0.8% vs 0.4%) (Table S10 ).

The discriminative ability of the two‐step strategies was similar in pre‐ and postmenopausal women, but the two‐step strategies were better calibrated in postmenopausal women (Figures S4–S9 , Table S11 ). The discriminative ability and the calibration of the two‐step strategies were similar in oncology centers and non‐oncology centers (Figures S10–S15 , Table S12 ).

Additional analyses The results of the additional analyses are shown in Table S13 and S14 and Figures S16–S21 . Omitting patients with uncertain tumor outcome from the analysis slightly increased the overall prevalence of malignancy compared with the primary analysis (22.1% vs 21.1%), but had minimal effect on discriminative performance and calibration. Our sensitivity analysis, in which we expanded the definition of uncertain outcome, resulted in 1419 (29%) tumors with uncertain outcome and an AUC of the two‐step strategy without CA125 of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.91–0.95; 95% PI, 0.82–0.98).

DISCUSSION We describe the diagnostic performance of the modified BDs and of a two‐step strategy using the modified BDs as a first step and ADNEX as a second step when applied to patients managed either surgically or conservatively. The results indicate that the modified BDs are applicable in almost 40% of patients with an adnexal mass, that the risk of malignancy is very low if a modified BD applies, and that the two‐step strategy has excellent discriminative performance and is reasonably well calibrated.

The study strengths include: first, the large sample size and high number of participating centers; second, the prospective ultrasound protocol with agreed ultrasound terms, definitions and measurement techniques; and finally, consecutive inclusion of patients managed either surgically or conservatively.

We acknowledge four limitations related to potential bias. First, we excluded all data from 19 centers because they did not fulfill our predefined quality criteria. This means that, like in any study, we cannot rule out selection bias on a center‐level. We made these exclusions to obtain data that was informative (excluding centers with limited recruitment), representative (excluding centers with non‐consecutive recruitment) and reliable (excluding centers with low‐quality data or centers that stopped participation). This also reduced the potential for attrition bias (exclusions on a patient‐level). Including other centers could have resulted in higher or lower performance due to case‐mix heterogeneity

31 . We do not expect our exclusion of centers to have resulted in an overestimation of diagnostic performance, because we do not expect the quality of the ultrasound examinations to be lower in the excluded than in the included centers. In a study on the same dataset, a sensitivity analysis using immediately operated patients from all 36 centers resulted in the same AUC for ADNEX as the primary analysis based on 17 centers 17 . Second, the tumor outcome was based on multiple reference standards (differential verification), and for a small group of patients, tumor outcome could not be determined due to conflicting information or insufficient follow‐up (partial verification)

29 . We addressed the potentially optimistic bias from partial and differential verification by using multiple imputation and a sensitivity analysis 27 . Model performance changed very little depending on the definition of uncertainty that we used. Third, 53% of the patients had a missing value for CA125. This affects the performance of ADNEX with CA125 but not that of the modified BDs or ADNEX without CA125. To deal with missing CA125 values, we used multiple imputation, which is the recommended approach to reduce bias due to missing values 18 ,
30 . Excluding cases with missing CA125 values is likely to bias AUCs downwards, because missing values are most common among tumors judged to be benign on ultrasound (Table S4 )

32 . The high number of missing values adds uncertainty to the results, and imputing multiple times acknowledges this as reflected in wider confidence intervals around performance estimates. Fourth, there was no blinding of examiners to previous information about the patient or of pathologists to clinical information. Imposing such blinding would be unethical and unrealistic. Lack of blinding may induce information bias when assessing predictors and detection bias when determining outcome based on histology. Information bias may lead to overestimation of performance (even though, importantly, the outcome was unknown at the inclusion scan when the predictors were assessed). We consider detection bias to be limited. Pathologists are unlikely to be influenced by preoperative ultrasound findings. This assumption is supported by findings in the IOTA Phase‐1 study, in which the results of central pathology review (blinded to clinical information) were highly similar to local results

8 . In summary, we used several recommended approaches to reduce bias. Information bias, an unavoidable clinical reality, may nevertheless have biased performance optimistically. This study is the first to evaluate the performance of the modified BDs, to suggest and evaluate the performance of a two‐step strategy using the modified BDs as a first step and ADNEX as a second step, and to do this in patients managed either surgically or conservatively. Three studies have externally validated a three‐step strategy using both the benign and malignant original simple descriptors as a first step, followed by the IOTA simple rules

10 as a second step and by subjective assessment by an expert as a final step. All three studies included patients managed either surgically or conservatively and showed the three‐step strategy to have excellent ability to discriminate between benign and malignant adnexal masses 33 , 34 , 35 . We believe that our two‐step strategy has advantages over the three‐step strategy: all tumors can be classified by a single ultrasound examiner, and a risk of malignancy is assigned to all tumors as well as a likelihood estimate of type of malignancy.

It is reassuring that the discriminative ability of ADNEX when applied to tumors to which the modified BDs do not apply was almost as good (AUC, 0.92 (with CA125) and 0.91 (without CA125)) as when ADNEX was applied on all tumors. When applied on all 4905 tumors, the AUC for ADNEX both with and without CA125 was 0.94 17 . Moreover, the discriminative performance of the two‐step strategies (AUC, 0.95 and 0.94) was similar to that of using ADNEX on all 4905 masses, and the clinical utility of the two‐step strategies was the same as that of applying ADNEX on all masses (Figure 4 ). This shows that using ADNEX on all masses has no advantage over using the two‐step strategy.

Two issues require further research. First, evaluating ultrasound images is affected by the level of experience of the examiner. The IOTA5 study involved mainly Level‐II and ‐III examiners. Even though previous studies have suggested that ADNEX works well also in the hands of less experienced examiners 36 , the role of experience should be investigated more explicitly. A large multicenter study, in which examiner experience is quantified before patient recruitment, could elucidate whether and how experience affects discrimination and calibration performance. Second, we observed heterogeneity between centers regarding discrimination and calibration for all models validated on IOTA Phase‐5 data
17 . When more data become available, it will be important to study possible reasons for this heterogeneity.

In conclusion, the two‐step strategy lends itself very well to clinical use. A large proportion of adnexal masses can be classified by the modified BDs as having a very low risk of malignancy without computer support. For the remaining masses, an estimate of risk of malignancy and type of malignancy can be obtained using the ADNEX model. An ADNEX calculator is available online and as an application for smartphones ( https://iotagroup.org/iota‐models‐software/adnex‐risk‐model ). It is also embedded in many ultrasound machines. This facilitates its use in clinical practice. The two‐step strategy can be used for patient counseling to individualize management. It could also be used to stratify patients into risk groups, such as the ovarian‐adnexal reporting and data system (O‐RADS) risk groups

37 . Risk stratification can facilitate selection of optimal management for patients with adnexal masses 38 . Hereditary tubo-ovarian cancer risk assessment has evolved from a BRCA1/2 -centered consultation to an integrated prevention pathway that begins at diagnosis and extends to unaffected relatives. Germline testing is now justified for patients with epithelial tubo-ovarian cancer because actionable pathogenic variants are common enough that family-history-only referral misses many carriers. The central clinical challenge is no longer whether testing matters, but whether testing is interpreted and implemented in a way that prevents cancer. BRCA1 and BRCA2 remain the highest-impact tubo-ovarian cancer predisposition genes, but Lynch syndrome genes, BRIP1, RAD51C, RAD51D, PALB2 , and selected rare histology-directed syndromes require distinct counseling. Gene-specific penetrance, age-specific risk, family history, comorbidities, reproductive plans, and menopause consequences should shape the timing of risk-reducing surgery. Tumor testing improves therapeutic selection and can identify possible hereditary variants, but tumor-only testing does not replace germline testing when hereditary evaluation is indicated. Cascade testing should be measured and resourced as part of tubo-ovarian cancer care rather than treated as a passive family responsibility. Mainstream testing, traceback programs, and navigation-supported cascade testing offer pragmatic implementation models, but access gaps remain.

For gynecologic oncology clinicians, modern hereditary risk assessment should be understood as a multidisciplinary prevention intervention: testing is the entry point, not the endpoint. The original clinical model - referral for BRCA1/2 counseling when the family history was striking - was appropriate for an earlier era of limited testing and narrower therapeutic relevance, but it is no longer sufficient. Multigene germline testing, tumor genomic testing, homologous recombination deficiency testing, and expanding risk-reducing surgical strategies have changed the clinical question from “Who qualifies for testing?” to “How does testing inform precise prevention for patients and relatives?” Current guidance from major oncology, pathology, and genetics organizations supports systematic testing after epithelial tubo-ovarian cancer and selected rare non-epithelial tumors with syndrome-specific associations, coordinated tumor-germline workflows, and gene-specific management of inherited risk. 1 - 5

The hereditary tubo-ovarian cancer risk assessment is not merely a laboratory exercise. It is a longitudinal prevention pathway that includes test selection, interpretation, counseling, risk-reducing surgery when appropriate, and cascade testing. When any component fails - a patient is not offered testing, a tumor-only result is misread as excluding inherited risk, a variant of uncertain significance is overinterpreted, or relatives are not supported to test - the preventive value of the pathway is lost. 2 , 6

Despite the evolving evidence base, a gap persists between guideline recommendations and clinical practice. Guidelines define who should be tested and how gene-specific risk should be managed, but translating that framework into a reliable prevention pathway — one that reaches patients, informs relatives, and adapts to implementation constraints — remains a practical challenge. This narrative review is intended as a clinical reference for physicians at the intersection of diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Its objective is to integrate gene-specific counseling, tumor–germline interpretation, prevention timing, cascade testing, and implementation strategies rather than to replace local or national guidelines.

Scope and approach This is a clinically oriented narrative review. We synthesize major international guidance, including major guideline recommendations, together with selected primary studies that clarify penetrance, test interpretation, prevention, and implementation. Guideline-based recommendations are distinguished from areas requiring individualized counseling, and jurisdiction-specific eligibility, consent, and management requirements remain applicable. We address the genes and syndromes most relevant to tubo-ovarian cancer diagnosis and prevention, the distinction between therapeutic and hereditary testing, interpretation of common result categories, gene-specific timing of risk-reducing surgery, limitations of risk models, and implementation strategies that can increase equitable access.

Why hereditary risk assessment matters in tubo-ovarian cancer prevention Tubo-ovarian cancer remains a lethal malignancy worldwide; GLOBOCAN 2022 estimated approximately 324,000 new cases and 207,000 deaths globally, reflecting both late-stage presentation and limited effectiveness of early detection at population level. 7 Inherited predisposition accounts for a clinically important fraction of epithelial tubo-ovarian cancer. Contemporary series 8 and guidelines estimate that approximately 15-20% of epithelial tubo-ovarian cancers are associated with pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variants in tubo-ovarian cancer susceptibility genes, most commonly BRCA1 and BRCA2 , but also RAD51C , RAD51D , BRIP1 , PALB2 , and the Lynch syndrome genes MLH1 , MSH2 , MSH6 , including EPCAM deletions that cause MSH2 silencing. 2 , 9 This prevalence is high enough to justify systematic germline testing rather than relying on family history alone.

Family history is an imperfect screening tool for hereditary risk. Small family size, paternal transmission, adoption, incomplete knowledge of relatives, early deaths, hysterectomy or oophorectomy in relatives, and under-documentation of cancer diagnoses all reduce sensitivity. Family-history criteria may also amplify disparities when access to accurate family history or genetic services differs across ancestry, language, geography, and socioeconomic status. 3 , 9 Beyond these limitations, the case for systematic testing extends to its direct clinical value: for the affected patient, germline results may influence treatment selection, second-cancer risk management, and eligibility for trials. For relatives, the same result may create the opportunity to prevent tubo-ovarian, breast, endometrial, colorectal, pancreatic, or prostate cancer depending on the gene. 10 , 11

Identifying carriers, however, is only valuable if it leads to action. Tubo-ovarian cancer screening is not an effective approach for prevention in high-risk carriers. Transvaginal ultrasonography and cancer antigen 125-based screening have not demonstrated a mortality benefit in the general population, including in the final UKCTOCS analysis, and have not established a survival benefit in high-risk carriers. Guidelines therefore regard such surveillance, if used, as an interim option for selected high-risk individuals who defer risk-reducing surgery rather than as a prevention strategy. 4 , 12 , 13 Therefore, the practical value of hereditary risk assessment is most evident when it enables risk-reducing surgery, breast and colorectal surveillance where indicated, chemoprevention or contraception discussions, reproductive counseling, and cascade testing.

Who should be tested and referred All patients with epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer should be offered germline genetic testing that includes BRCA1 and BRCA2, and if available, other clinically relevant ovarian cancer susceptibility genes, including BRIP1 , RAD51C , RAD51D , PALB2 , MLH1 , MSH2 , MSH6 , and PMS2 . 1 - 3 , 5 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) recommends germline testing for all women diagnosed with epithelial ovarian cancer and somatic tumor testing for BRCA1/2 in those without a germline pathogenic variant; it also recommends mismatch repair deficiency testing for clear cell, endometrioid, or mucinous ovarian cancers. 2 The 2024 Society of Gynecologic Oncology clinical practice statement is concordant and emphasizes coordinated germline and somatic testing, while ACOG recommends routine hereditary cancer risk assessment and referral when increased risk is identified. 14 , 15 The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) similarly recommends pre-test counseling and germline testing for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer and for rare ovarian tumors with specific hereditary associations, including Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, small cell carcinoma of the ovary hypercalcemic type, ovarian sex cord tumor with annular tubules, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the ovary, and gynandroblastoma. 3 ESMO and the ESGO-ESMO-ESP consensus likewise support systematic germline testing and coordinated molecular assessment in epithelial tubo-ovarian cancer. 4 , 16 Borderline ovarian tumors are not, by themselves, a universal indication for germline testing; testing should instead be guided by personal and family history, tumor features, and jurisdiction-specific recommendations. 17

Referral pathways should be broader than the test order itself and should define responsibility at each step. In a mainstream testing model, the treating gynecologic oncology team may initiate pre-test education, obtain consent according to local requirements, order germline testing, document the test indication and result in the oncology record, and ensure that results are communicated to the patient and relevant clinicians. However, mainstream testing should not replace genetics expertise. Genetics professionals should be involved for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, variants of uncertain significance that affect counseling, discordant tumor–germline results, negative results despite a strong or verified family history, rare tumors suggesting a syndrome-specific workup, complex reproductive or risk-reducing surgery decisions, and any situation in which the treating team cannot provide gene-specific counseling. Importantly, variants of uncertain significance should not be used to guide risk-reducing surgery or predictive testing in relatives unless reclassified. Finally, referral pathways should define how confirmed hereditary findings will be translated into cascade testing for at-risk relatives, while also specifying how unaffected individuals should be evaluated when no familial pathogenic variant is known but the cancer pattern in the family or risk-model estimates still suggest inherited risk. 1 , 3

In practice, the most important quality metric is not simply whether testing is available. It is whether every eligible patient receives a clear recommendation, can access testing in a timely manner, receives an interpretable result, and has a route for relatives to act on it. Population-based testing in unaffected individuals without a known familial pathogenic variant is a separate question from universal testing after a cancer diagnosis. Such programs can identify carriers missed by family-history criteria, but eligibility, panel composition, consent, downstream capacity, and cost-effectiveness depend on the population and health system. 9

Tubo-ovarian cancer predisposition genes and syndromes BRCA1 and BRCA2 BRCA1 and BRCA2 remain the highest-impact tubo-ovarian cancer predisposition genes, but counseling should present penetrance as an age-dependent estimate rather than a fixed individual risk. In a large prospective analysis of BRCA1/2 carriers, the cumulative tubo-ovarian cancer risk to age 80 years was estimated at 44% for BRCA1 carriers and 17% for BRCA2 carriers, while cumulative breast cancer risk to age 80 years was 72% and 69%, respectively . 18 These estimates have uncertainty around them, are influenced by the carrier populations studied, and do not imply uniform risk across the life course.

Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy is associated with substantial reduction in ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancer risk and with reduced mortality in BRCA1/2 carriers. 19 , 20 Because BRCA1 -associated risk rises earlier, discussion of surgery generally begins after childbearing at age 35–40 years for BRCA1 pathogenic variant carriers and age 40–45 years for BRCA2 pathogenic variant carriers. The precise timing, however, should be individualized by integrating age, family history, prior cancer history, reproductive plans, and comorbidities rather than applying a fixed threshold. The consequences of premenopausal oophorectomy—including vasomotor symptoms, sexual dysfunction, bone loss, cardiovascular and cognitive concerns, infertility, and psychological effects—require explicit discussion before surgery. Hormone therapy after premenopausal risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy should be individualized in specialist counseling. Decisions should account for personal breast cancer history, breast tumor hormone receptor status when applicable, uterus status and the need for progestin with systemic estrogen, contraindications to hormone therapy, route and dose, severity of menopausal symptoms, bone and cardiovascular health, and patient preferences. In BRCA1/2 carriers without contraindications and without a personal history of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, hormone therapy until the average age of natural menopause may be considered after individualized risk–benefit counseling, and can start early after surgery. 4 , 12

Lynch syndrome genes: MLH1, MSH2/EPCAM, MSH6, PMS2 Lynch syndrome counseling must be gene specific. Prospective Lynch Syndrome Database data demonstrated that gynecologic cancer risks differ materially across mismatch repair genes, with ovarian cancer risk generally higher for MLH1 and MSH2 , variable for MSH6 , and lower or uncertain for PMS2 . 21 , 22 In the 2020 gene-specific Prospective Lynch Syndrome Database analysis, cumulative ovarian cancer incidence to age 75 years was approximately 11% for MLH1 , 17% for MSH2 , 11% for MSH6 , and 3% for PMS2 , although confidence intervals were wide for some estimates. 21

EPCAM deletions that involve the 3′ end can permit transcriptional read-through into MSH2 and cause allele-specific MSH2 promoter hypermethylation; cancer risk varies with deletion size and location, so interpretation requires genetics expertise. 23 Co-occurring pathogenic variants in BRCA1/2 and a mismatch repair gene are rare; available case-series data suggest that each syndrome should be interpreted and managed on its own evidence base. 24 Synchronous endometrial and ovarian cancers, particularly endometrioid tumors, are enriched for mismatch repair deficiency and Lynch syndrome and should prompt tumor mismatch repair assessment and germline evaluation when indicated. 25

Risk-reducing gynecologic surgery for Lynch syndrome differs from BRCA -associated prevention because endometrial cancer prevention is a central objective and ovarian cancer risk is more gene-dependent. Hysterectomy after completion of childbearing is commonly discussed to reduce endometrial cancer risk, particularly for carriers of pathogenic variants of MLH1, MSH2, and EPCAM deletions, often from the mid-to-late thirties, with later or more individualized timing for MSH6 and PMS2, and adjustment for family history, colorectal cancer history, surgical history, and patient preferences. The decision to add bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy should be considered separately from hysterectomy rather than assumed as a combined operation. Oophorectomy counseling should reflect gene-specific ovarian cancer risk, menopausal consequences, and competing health priorities: it may be more strongly considered for MLH1 and MSH2 / EPCAM carriers, individualized for MSH6 carriers, and approached with caution for PMS2 carriers because ovarian cancer risk may be near population level. 3 , 4 , 12 Thus, Lynch syndrome counseling should distinguish hysterectomy for endometrial cancer prevention from oophorectomy for ovarian cancer prevention, rather than treating both procedures as a uniform recommendation across all mismatch repair genes.

BRIP1, RAD51C, and RAD51D BRIP1 , RAD51C , and RAD51D are moderate-penetrance tubo-ovarian cancer predisposition genes, and prevention counseling should be age-specific, family-contextual, and explicit about uncertainty. Yang and colleagues estimated cumulative ovarian cancer risks to age 80 years of 11% for RAD51C carriers (95% CI, 6–21%) and 13% for RAD51D carriers (95% CI, 7–23%); risk was higher in carriers with a strong family history of ovarian cancer and was largely concentrated after age 50 years. 26

BRIP1 is also associated with a moderate increase in epithelial ovarian cancer risk, with an estimated cumulative risk to age 80 years of 5.8% (95% CI, 3.6–9.1%), although estimates vary by study design and may be modified by family history and ascertainment context. 27 These estimates support gene-specific counseling but should not be extrapolated to BRCA1 -equivalent surgical timing.

The clinical implication is not that these genes should be managed exactly like BRCA1 . Rather, carriers should be offered counseling about risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after completion of childbearing, often around age 45-50 years, with adjustment for family history, ancestry, comorbidity, prior breast cancer, and patient values. Earlier surgery may be reasonable in selected families with unusually early ovarian cancer, but genotype alone rarely justifies BRCA1 -like timing. 4 , 12 , 28 , 29

PALB2 PALB2 is a clinically important homologous recombination gene, particularly for breast cancer risk, however, current evidence does not support treating PALB2 as BRCA -equivalent for ovarian cancer.. An international family study estimated PALB2 -associated breast cancer risk to age 80 years at 53% and ovarian cancer risk at 5%. 30 The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) PALB2 Practice Resource therefore supports personalized management that considers family history and acknowledges a substantially lower ovarian cancer risk than for BRCA1/2 . 31 For tubo-ovarian prevention, PALB2 counseling often centers on whether the individual lifetime tubo-ovarian cancer risk exceeds a prevention threshold and whether surgery is being considered near or after the natural age of menopause. 4 , 28 , 31

Genes with limited ovarian cancer actionability: ATM ATM is a useful example of why gene lists must not be converted into automatic surgical indications. ATM pathogenic variants are established primarily as breast cancer predisposition variants, while ovarian cancer risk estimates remain low, inconsistent, or insufficient to support genotype-alone risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy. 4 , 12 , 32 A patient with an ATM pathogenic variant and a strong family history of ovarian cancer may still warrant individualized risk modeling or specialist review, but the indication is not the ATM result in isolation.

Rare histology-directed syndromes: DICER1 , SMARCA4 , STK11 /Peutz-Jeghers syndrome Rare ovarian histologies may provide stronger clues to an underlying hereditary syndrome than testing strategies designed primarily around common epithelial ovarian cancers. DICER1 tumor predisposition is associated with ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors and gynandroblastoma, as well as embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, pleuropulmonary blastoma, thyroid disease, and other manifestations. For these tumors, DICER1 assessment could be performed by immunohistochemistry or by molecular testing, and a pathogenic finding or suggestive phenotype should prompt germline evaluation. 33 , 34 Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type, is characterized by SMARCA4 inactivation; loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression by immunohistochemistry can support the diagnosis, and germline SMARCA4 evaluation is indicated for affected patients, with cascade testing for relatives when a germline pathogenic variant is confirmed. 35 , 36 Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in STK11 , is associated with sex cord tumor with annular tubules and a broader cancer spectrum involving the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, breast, cervix, and other gynecologic sites. 37 Together, these entities highlight that hereditary ovarian cancer assessment should extend beyond high-grade serous carcinoma and incorporate histology-directed evaluation when rare tumor types are encountered ( Table 1 ).

Pre-test counseling and test selection Pre-test counseling should answer three practical questions: why testing is recommended, what results may mean, and how results may affect treatment and relatives. Counseling should cover the genes included, the distinction between germline and tumor testing, the possibility of pathogenic, negative, or uncertain results, privacy and insurance considerations applicable to the jurisdiction, and reproductive options. Counseling can be delivered by genetics professionals or by trained oncology teams within a mainstream model, provided escalation pathways exist for complex cases. 38 - 40

Panel selection should be driven by clinical utility. For epithelial ovarian cancer, panels generally include established or clinically relevant ovarian susceptibility genes: BRCA1 , BRCA2 , BRIP1 , RAD51C , RAD51D , PALB2 , MLH1 , MSH2, MSH6 , and PMS2 , with EPCAM deletion analysis where relevant. Genes such as ATM may appear on broader hereditary cancer panels because of associations with other cancers, but current ovarian risk evidence does not support ovarian surgery based on ATM alone. Broader panels may be reasonable when histology, age, personal history, or family history suggests another syndrome, but indiscriminate expansion increases the likelihood of uncertain findings and includes genes with unclear management. Test selection should also consider whether the patient has had prior single-gene testing; many patients tested years ago may not have had large rearrangement analysis or contemporary multigene panel testing. 2 , 10 , 41 , 42

Tumor testing versus germline testing Tumor testing and germline testing answer overlapping but distinct questions. Tumor testing identifies somatic and potential germline alterations that may guide therapy, particularly BRCA1/2 status and homologous recombination deficiency in high-grade non-mucinous disease. 5 , 16 , 43 Germline testing determines inherited risk and is the basis for predictive testing of relatives. A tumor BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant should prompt evaluation for germline origin unless prior germline testing has already clarified this. Conversely, a negative tumor test does not reliably exclude a germline pathogenic variant because tumor assays vary in gene coverage, copy-number detection, sample adequacy and tumor purity, intratumoral heterogeneity or subclonality, allele-fraction thresholds, and bioinformatic filtering and reporting rules. 2 , 5 , 43 Prospective implementation data support parallel approaches. In the SIGNPOST study, 303 of 310 eligible patients underwent parallel germline and somatic testing; germline pathogenic variants were identified in BRCA1/2 in 47 patients (15.5%) and in RAD51C/RAD51D/BRIP1 in 7 patients (2.3%). A somatic-first BRCA strategy would have missed 20% of germline pathogenic variants, including large genomic rearrangements not detected by tumor testing. 44

Tumor-only testing therefore does not replace germline testing when hereditary evaluation is indicated. This distinction should be explicit in multidisciplinary pathways: pathology and oncology workflows can identify therapeutic biomarkers rapidly, but hereditary assessment requires consent, germline assay selection, disclosure planning, documentation, and cascade testing.

Consent models for tumor testing are part of implementation rather than a peripheral administrative issue. Reflex tumor testing may reduce delays, but patients should receive clear information, an opportunity to ask questions, and an opt-out route where local governance supports this approach. In a 2025 UK study involving ovarian cancer patients, clinicians, and charity representatives, 33 of 34 patients (97%) considered reflex tumor testing acceptable, if information and opt-out options were available; this evidence supports pathway redesign but does not remove the need for informed consent for germline testing. 45

Post-test interpretation Pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants Pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants are clinically actionable when the gene-disease association is established, and management recommendations exist. Actionability includes gene-specific cancer risk counseling, risk-reducing surgery where indicated, breast or colorectal surveillance, treatment implications, reproductive options, and cascade testing. The result should be communicated with the gene, variant, inheritance pattern, cancer spectrum, and recommended next steps documented in a way that other clinicians can interpret.

True-negative results A true-negative result occurs when a relative tests negative for a known familial pathogenic variant. This is usually reassuring for the cancers associated with that familial variant, although general population screening and risk factors still apply. The concept should not be confused with a negative multigene panel in an affected proband when no familial variant is known. 46 , 47

Uninformative negative results An uninformative negative result in an affected patient reduces the probability of a currently detectable hereditary syndrome but does not erase familial risk. 46 Residual risk may reflect undiscovered genes or regulatory and noncoding variants not captured by the assay, low-level mosaicism below the assay’s detection or reporting threshold, structural variants missed by older methods, polygenic risk, shared environment, or chance. When suspicion remains high, genetics review may consider updated sequencing, copy-number analysis, tumor-informed testing, or testing of another tissue. Management should return to personal and family history, tumor features, and updated testing availability. 48 , 49

Variants of uncertain significance Variants of uncertain significance are a predictable by-product of multigene testing and must be handled with discipline. The ACMG and the Association of Molecular Pathology (AMP) standards state that a variant of uncertain significance should not be used in clinical decision-making. 50 In hereditary cancer testing, reclassification of variants of uncertain significance occurs over time, but the probability depends on the laboratory, genes tested, variant type, ancestry representation in reference data, and duration of follow-up. In a retrospective cohort from a single commercial hereditary cancer testing laboratory, including 1.45 million individuals and 1.67 million initial tests, Mersch and colleagues found that 7.7% of unique variants of uncertain significance were reclassified; 91.2% of those unique reclassified variants of uncertain significance were downgraded to benign or likely benign, and 8.7% were upgraded to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. 51 Because many variants were observed in more than one individual, 24.9% of all reported variants of uncertain significance observations—not 24.9% of patients—were reclassified. No universally accepted fixed re-review interval applies across laboratories. Reassessment should follow the testing laboratory’s classification and recontact policy and may be triggered by laboratory updates, new family or tumor information, or a management decision that depends on the result. Variants of uncertain significance should not guide risk-reducing surgery or predictive testing of relatives unless reclassified ( Table 2 ).

The clinical response is therefore conservative: do not recommend risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, mastectomy, intensified screening, or predictive testing of unaffected relatives based on a variant of uncertain significance alone. Relatives with cancer may sometimes be tested in segregation studies coordinated by genetics professionals, but that is different from predictive testing for management. Patients should be told that recontact processes vary and that they should keep contact details current, and should return to genetics if relevant family history changes. 50

Gene-specific risk stratification and timing of prevention Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy is the most effective established ovarian cancer prevention strategy for carriers whose risk exceeds accepted thresholds, but timing should be individualized. A prevention threshold of approximately 4-5% lifetime ovarian cancer risk has been supported by cost-effectiveness analyses and incorporated into several recommendations. 3 , 12 , 52 That threshold is a starting point for shared decision-making, not an automatic surgical mandate.

For BRCA1 pathogenic variant carriers, risk generally justifies discussion of surgery after childbearing and often from age 35-40 years. For BRCA2 carriers, the later age distribution supports discussion from about age 40-45 years. For RAD51C , RAD51D , BRIP1 , and PALB2 , counseling frequently centers on surgery around age 45-50 years or later, modified by family history and modeled risk. 1 , 3 , 4 , 12 , 26 - 30 For Lynch syndrome, hysterectomy and oophorectomy should be considered as separate prevention decisions: hysterectomy is central for endometrial cancer prevention, while the decision to add bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is strongest for MLH1 and MSH2 / EPCAM , individualized for MSH6 , and more conservative for PMS2 . 1 , 3 , 12 , 21 , 22 After natural menopause, the balance may favor oophorectomy because premature-menopause harms no longer apply, but the indication should still reflect gene-specific residual risk, prior surgery, comorbidity, and patient preferences.

Risk-reducing early salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy is attractive because many high-grade serous carcinomas arise in the distal fallopian tube and because delayed oophorectomy may reduce premature menopause. However, it remains investigational because long-term cancer prevention efficacy is not yet established. This strategy should not be conflated with opportunistic salpingectomy during benign pelvic surgery in average-risk patients; opportunistic salpingectomy does not address the residual hereditary ovarian and peritoneal risk created by delaying oophorectomy. Major prospective studies include TUBA-WISP II, which compares salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy against standard salpingo-oophorectomy in high-risk carriers, and NRG-CC008/SOROCk, which evaluates noninferiority of salpingectomy to salpingo-oophorectomy for risk reduction in BRCA1 carriers. 53 Until prospective data demonstrate that salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy provides comparable tubo-ovarian cancer prevention, this approach should not be presented as equivalent to risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy and should generally be offered only within a research protocol or structured registry with explicit counseling about residual ovarian and peritoneal cancer risk. 1 , 4 , 12

Role and limitations of individualized risk models Risk models can improve counseling when gene-specific risk is modified by family history, competing risks, and non-genetic factors. BOADICEA, implemented through CanRisk, estimates carrier probabilities and breast, ovarian, and other cancer risks using family history, pathogenic variants, polygenic risk scores, and other factors. 54 , 55 The epithelial tubo-ovarian cancer component incorporates pathogenic variants in BRCA1 , BRCA2 , RAD51C , RAD51D , and BRIP1 , a polygenic risk score, epidemiologic factors, and family history. 56 A 2024 UK Biobank validation reported good calibration for 10-year epithelial tubo-ovarian cancer risk, with improved discrimination when questionnaire-based factors, family history, a 36-variant polygenic risk score, and pathogenic variants were added. 57 Other similar tools answer different clinical questions: BCRAT/Gail and IBIS/Tyrer-Cuzick primarily estimate breast cancer risk, whereas BRCAPRO and Penn II primarily estimate BRCA1/2 carrier probability. They may support breast-risk counseling or testing referral but are not substitutes for ovarian cancer risk models when considering risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy. 58

The utility of CanRisk/BOADICEA is greatest when the model clarifies whether a moderate-penetrance carrier or a patient with familial risk is likely to cross a prevention threshold. Model outputs are conditional estimates, not direct measurements of individual risk. They depend on complete family history, correct variant classification, ancestry-specific calibration, population incidence, competing mortality, and available clinical and reproductive factors. Polygenic risk scores add uncertainty because performance is best established in the populations in which they were developed and their effect sizes are more modest than those of high-penetrance pathogenic variants. 54 - 57 , 59 Models should therefore support, not replace, expert clinical judgment and shared decision-making.

Cascade testing and family communication Cascade testing should be treated as a measurable implementation outcome of ovarian cancer genetic testing pathways. A pathogenic variant identified in an affected patient creates a 50% prior probability for each first-degree relative in autosomal dominant syndromes, before considering family structure and intervening test results. Relatives who test positive can receive targeted prevention; relatives who test true negative can often avoid unnecessary high-risk interventions. 11

The traditional model relies heavily on the proband to inform relatives. This protects privacy but produces inconsistent completion of cascade genetic testing among at-risk relatives. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer families, Ahsan and colleagues included 30 studies in the meta-analysis and reported pooled cascade genetic testing uptake of 33% among at-risk relatives (95% CI, 25%–42%), with higher uptake among female relatives and first-degree relatives. 60 This estimate refers to completion of cascade genetic testing, not merely family communication or attendance at counseling. Barriers include grief, family estrangement, limited health literacy, uncertainty about what to say, cost, geography, privacy constraints, and failure to treat cascade testing as a measurable outcome of hereditary cancer care. Effective programs use written family letters, genetic counseling support, navigator follow-up, direct contact of relatives where legally and ethically permitted, electronic health record prompts, and low-friction targeted testing. 60 - 63

Implementation models Mainstream genetic testing In traditional referral models, patients are usually sent to genetics services for all steps of the testing process — counseling, consent, ordering, and result disclosure — which creates delays and limits reach. Mainstream genetic testing replaces this by embedding pre-test counseling and test ordering within oncology clinics, reserving genetics input for complex cases. This model is particularly appropriate in ovarian cancer because testing has immediate therapeutic and hereditary relevance. Studies of mainstream pathways in ovarian cancer show that trained oncology teams can deliver testing with acceptable patient-reported outcomes and higher reach than genetics-only referral models. 38 - 40 , 44 In a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of mainstream genetic testing at or after cancer diagnosis, pooled testing uptake was 91% across cancer types and 93% among ovarian cancer cohorts, with high satisfaction and low decisional conflict, regret, and post-test distress. 39 Economic modeling also supports unselected multigene germline and somatic testing in epithelial ovarian cancer compared with family-history-based approaches, supporting the clinical and economic case for universal testing. 64 Mainstreaming should not mean diluted counseling; it should mean standardized information, clear consent, rapid testing, and reliable genetics backup.

Traceback programs Traceback programs identify patients or families affected by ovarian cancer before universal testing became routine and offer genetic testing retrospectively. These programs are prevention-oriented because many probands are years from diagnosis or deceased; relatives may be the main beneficiaries. Traceback studies demonstrate feasibility but also show that contact, consent, and uptake are challenging, making registry linkage, survivor-sensitive communication, and navigation essential. 61 , 62

Navigation-supported cascade testing Navigation-supported cascade testing treats family follow-up as a care process rather than a passive recommendation. Navigators can help patients understand the result, identify relatives, generate family letters, address cost and insurance barriers, track referrals, and recontact families. Randomized and implementation studies suggest that facilitation can improve communication and testing compared with usual care, although optimal models vary by legal context and health system. 60 , 63

Access issues and underserved populations The impact of the models depends on equitable reach. Implementation failures should be viewed as modifiable system problems. Lack of provider recommendation, referral leakage, long waits, high out-of-pocket cost, language discordance, low digital access, medical mistrust, and limited culturally concordant counseling are not patient deficits; they are design failures. NICE explicitly frames services as responsible for inclusive pathways, training, information, and support for underserved communities. 3 Equity-oriented programs should measure offer rate, completion rate, pathogenic variant detection, time to result, cascade testing uptake, and risk-reducing intervention uptake by ancestry, language, deprivation, geography, and disability status.

Future directions The next phase of hereditary ovarian cancer prevention should integrate diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and family prevention into a single measurable pathway. First, germline and tumor testing workflows should be coordinated so that treatment biomarkers do not obscure hereditary evaluation. Second, gene-specific risk estimates require continued refinement, especially for moderate-penetrance genes, non-European ancestry groups, and individuals with limited family history. Third, risk-reducing salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy should continue to be evaluated in adequately powered studies with long-term cancer incidence, quality-of-life, sexual function, menopause, and adherence outcomes to provide high-quality evidence to inform recommendations.

Fourth, risk models need transparent validation across ancestries and clinical settings before polygenic risk scores are used to make high-stakes surgical decisions. Fifth, cascade testing should be recognized as an outcome of ovarian cancer care and supported with infrastructure, not left to chance. Finally, rare histology-directed syndromes require better integration between pathologists, gynecologic oncologists, pediatric and adolescent gynecology, geneticists, and family cancer clinics. Figure 2 .

Conclusions Hereditary ovarian cancer risk assessment has evolved from BRCA1/2-focused counseling into a prevention pathway linking tumor diagnosis to at-risk relatives. Current guideline-based practice is increasingly systematic, gene-specific, and implementation-focused: recognizing BRCA1/2 as central but not exclusive, treating Lynch syndrome by gene, distinguishing moderate- from high-penetrance genes and avoiding over management of variants of uncertain significance or low-evidence genes. Cascade testing should be embedded into ovarian cancer care rather than left as an optional downstream step. For gynecologic oncology clinicians, genetic testing is the entry point; prevention is the goal.

Purpose To evaluate the association of surgical quality and survival in patients with advanced ovarian cancer in a real-world setting.

Methods This population-based registry study analysed FIGO stage III/IV ovarian cancer patients in Hamburg, Germany (2014–2024). Patients were categorized by surgical outcome (no macroscopic residuals vs. macroscopic residuals). Kaplan–Meier functions and Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations with survival outcomes.

Results The cohort comprised 576 patients (median age 65 years, median follow-up 57 months). No macroscopic residuals were achieved in 370 patients (64.2%). In multivariable analysis, no macroscopic residuals were associated with reduced mortality risk (HR 0.62, 95% CI: 0.42–0.90) and reduced progression risk (HR 0.68, 95% CI: 0.49–0.94). Advanced FIGO stage, poor performance status, and increasing age were independent predictors of worse outcomes.

Conclusion Achieving no macroscopic residuals remains a critical prognostic factor in advanced ovarian cancer. The rate of 64.2% demonstrates that optimal surgical outcomes are achievable in routine practice, though opportunities for improvement remain compared to specialized centres.
